meta.title: Lawn Mowing Experiment
meta.description: This is a story about how our minds work.
meta.byline: By Russell Samora, Arjun Kakkar, Florina Sutanto, and Sushant Karki

content.value: Mowing a lawn. Vacuuming a room. Shoveling snow. You’ve probably done these tasks hundreds of times without thinking much about it. Some part of your brain works out a route that’s usually good enough to get the job done. People are actually pretty good at this, and better than you’d guess for a problem that is hard for computers. We wanted to see it for ourselves, so we built a lawn and asked people to mow it.

value.prompt: Give it a try. How efficiently can you mow this lawn?
value.played: A little while ago, you mowed this lawn. Here’s a replay.

value.b2: The most efficient path is just
value.skip: You skipped the game, so here is just the optimal path. Is this what you would’ve done?
value.strip: If we strip away the grass, mowing is really just a path of connected squares.

content.value: A few weeks ago, 20,305 people mowed the same lawn. Here is what they look like.
Many came close to the optimal path. 55% of people came within five moves of the best possible path, and <mark>18% did it perfectly.</mark>

Many different approaches, yet similar, pretty good outcomes. Only 49 squares needed to be covered, but people found 9,640 different ways to do it. Despite all that variety, the median person still hit 91% efficiency (within 5 moves).
For this small lawn, there were 12 different perfect solutions and people found them all.
But what were you actually solving?
Finding the best path through the squares is a classic computer science problem. No, don’t leave! We promise this won’t get too wonky.
Path planning problems
Solving the lawn mowing problem is formally called Coverage Path Planning, and is related to one of the most famous path planning problems in computer science: The Traveling Salesman Problem.

value.figcaption: From The Coding Train with Daniel Shiffman

content.value: The premise is simple: a salesman must visit a set of cities exactly once and return to their starting point, all while taking the shortest possible route. We see this all the time in the real world. A pizza delivery driver planning their stops or a trick-or-treater maximizing their candy haul is solving a version of this problem.

We wanted to create this mowing experiment after we read a study that found humans come impressively close to computer-calculated optimal solutions to this problem with fewer stops, and even do pretty good — just 11% less efficient than optimal — for 70+ stops. But as the stops increase, humans’ ability decreases. Would results be similar for mowing a lawn?

value.alt: A chart depicting how people perform on the Traveling Salesman Problem compared to the optimal path, which shows that people perform near-ideal at fewer nodes, with a slow increasing deviation as more nodes are added
value.figcaption: Chart of findings from this study

content.value: A slight detour, if we may. It is worth noting that there are two main ways to tackle a problem like this:

li: algorithms which calculate the optimal path and
heuristics which are simple strategies to complete the path

content.value: Why do we need heuristics? If we look at the brute force calculations for a salesperson visiting just 10 cities, we’d surprisingly need to test 3.6 million possible routes. That number explodes exponentially as more cities are added.
15 cities and we’re at 1.3 trillion possible routes. 😱
20 cities balloons to 2.4 quintillion possible routes. 🤯

When problems are small, the approach doesn’t matter much, almost everything works. But as complexity grows, optimal becomes impossible and heuristics become necessary. This is true for both humans and computers. We both fall back on good-enough strategies when perfect is impractical.
With the maths out of the way we can get back to the good stuff.
A guided tour

steps.text: Let’s replay a mowing session, director’s-cut style, with some commentary along the way. For this walkthrough, we’ll use a perfectly average run from player yo7m5rr3nl, who called themselves Bones. It took them 54 moves–five more than optimal. We recorded the timestamp of each move, so every hesitation or direction change left a data footprint.
steps.note: Just the trace of the path (use xray, not realtime) - path yo7m5rr3nl

steps.text: We’ll rewind to the start and walk through it. Before Bones even makes a move, they pause for 2.9 seconds. They were perfectly average here as well; the median first-move pause for all players was three seconds. Upon seeing the grid revealed, they naturally pause to survey the lawn and, perhaps, make a plan.
steps.note: back to lawn; don’t play inline-mini chart of first-move pause time histogram?

steps.text: Off goes Bones! They have nothing to decide in the opening stretch until the fifth square. Continue right, or go down?
steps.note: play quick animation until fifth square, then overlay grid of blinking square options (5,0 and 4,1)

steps.text: This is where players’ paths first diverge. Bones barely hesitates (0.7s) and decides to go down, just like X% of players. This is a critical moment that we’ll come back to shortly.
steps.note: introduce forking; viz tk (maybe fork viz of everyone)

steps.text: They plod along the outside edge until they reach the bottom. Their first real pause (2.4s) comes when they realize they’ve hit a dead end and will have to retrace their steps.
steps.note: animate lawn from this point on, then show heatmap of pause duration (of the player’s path, up to this point) and hide lawn

steps.text: After realizing their mistake, they turn around and re-mow their first square to finish this section. To get to the other open section they must backtrack through two more squares. Then it is pretty much smooth sailing where they work around the edges first, then fill in the remaining squares in the middle.
steps.note: show lawn, animate remainder of path

steps.text: What differentiated the great players from everyone else comes down to a single critical mistake. We can divide the lawn into two main sections: left and right. Like most players, Bones chose to complete the left section first, forcing an inevitable backtrack because of this one-way corridor.
steps.note: left/right divide graphic and highlight the corridor

steps.text: If we look at where every player ended up we can see this play out. Players who were three or more moves from optimal finished all over the lawn.
steps.note: heatmap of other finishing spots on the right side

steps.text: While those who were nearly or perfectly optimal chose to mow the right side first so they could end their run on the left side, having anticipated the one-way trap.
steps.note: heatmap of other finishing spots on the left side

steps.text: One of those was player X. We tracked them down–discovered their name was X–and asked them, why were they so awesome at this game?

steps.note: question about snaking (required in lots of places which is counterintuitive to natural tendency to follow edges)

content.value: exit scrolly

We learned all of that from just one lawn. In our experiment, we tested players with five other grids at varying difficulty levels, giving us a fuller picture of how people approached pathfinding across larger and increasingly complicated problems.
show aggregate heatmap of all grids
First, here is everyone’s average optimality score across all the rounds they played. We measured optimality by counting the number of overlaps they made compared to the perfect optimal path.
histogram of average optimality by player; player average score highlighted
Now let’s answer the initial driving question: did optimality decrease as the problem size increased? No!
viz (slopegraph?) of optimality across rounds – all players and popular average

Our results showed that optimality held at ~90% (TKTK fact check) even as the lawn scaled from 25 cells to 196—almost 8x larger. This was surprising to us as we expected human optimality to break down as the problem grew more complicated, based on what we learned from the Traveling Salesman Problem.

We think this is because the consistent visual structure of our game allowed players to more easily draw on common heuristics compared to those who had to connect the random scattered nodes of the TSP. We believe our game supported two particular strategies: decomposition and compression. Players were able to decompose the grid into smaller, more manageable sections and solve them incrementally—clear this empty space first, then that corner, and finally the cavity between the rocks. As they moved between rounds, they compressed what they learned into a mental model of the game, allowing them to identify patterns in more complex grids and adapt their gameplay. Trap me once, shame on me; trap me twice…

That being said, we also think we might not have hit the true ceiling with our largest 14x14 grid. Did we underestimate how dedicated people were to the art of mowing? If we had continued to scale the grid, it's unclear whether we'd continue to see the same trend in optimality or whether we would eventually see it decline anyway.

What about speed? The obvious theory here is that players who took more time to think tended to do better, because they were able to carefully plan their moves. We looked at each player’s pause time and compared it against their optimality score.
Plot total pause time against efficiency and the relationship is flat.
scatter, total pause time vs efficiency, flat trend, Bones highlighted
It turns out that staring at the lawn longer did not make people meaningfully better at mowing it.
So thinking did not improve the score much, but it happened exactly where the problem got hard. If pausing does not help, then why does anyone win?

The best solvers were not the fastest, and they were not the longest thinkers. Speed alone did not predict a good path. Neither did total thinking time. What set the top solvers apart was where they spent their attention.

Some players, like X, planned ahead and were able to roughly anticipate where they should start and end, minimizing backtracking. Others made strategic pauses at ambiguous forks to analyze several moves ahead.

They moved at about the same pace as everyone else, sometimes slower, but they revisited far fewer squares. They were not burning effort everywhere. They spent it at the forks and cruised through the rest.
<mark>two ghost mowers side by side on the same clock, top solver vs average reader</mark>

So it is not about thinking more, or thinking faster. It is about when you think. And that is exactly what a good heuristic does: it saves your effort for the decisions that matter and spends nothing on the ones that do not.
